articles.title: A protein older than blood circulation could transform cancer immunotherapy
articles.summary: A protein that evolved long before the human circulatory system may help unlock stronger cancer treatments. When C3 is produced inside tumors, it blocks immune-suppressing cells and gives immunotherapy a better chance to work. Researchers were even able to recreate this effect in resistant tumors, significantly improving survival in mice.
articles.content:
An immune molecule that appeared in evolution long before blood circulation may help improve cancer immunotherapy. Scientists at Nagoya University in Japan discovered that complement C3 can prevent immune-suppressing cells from building up inside tumors, but only when the protein is produced locally within the tumor. C3 traveling through the bloodstream did not influence how well treatment worked.

The findings, published in Nature Communications, suggest that reproducing this local effect could benefit patients whose tumors do not produce enough C3 naturally.

An Ancient Part of the Immune System

C3 is an evolutionarily ancient protein found even in simple animals such as sponges and jellyfish. Most C3 is made in the liver and released into the bloodstream, where it helps the immune system defend the body against infections.

Scientists know much less about what C3 does when it is produced directly inside tissues and organs.

"Cancer tumors are surrounded by normal cells called fibroblasts. Until now, the role of complement C3 produced by these cancer-associated fibroblasts within tumor tissue was not known," said lead author Yuki Miyai, assistant professor at the Graduate School of Medicine, Nagoya University.

Local C3 Helps the Immune System Reach Tumors

The researchers found that C3 made within tumor tissue prevents immunosuppressive myeloid cells from entering the tumor microenvironment. These cells can weaken the body's ability to attack cancer. By keeping them out, locally produced C3 gives the immune system a better opportunity to recognize and fight tumor cells.

The results point to C3 as an important regulator of cancer immunotherapy, a form of treatment that helps the immune system identify and attack cancer cells.

To determine whether C3 in the bloodstream also affected immunotherapy, the team conducted experiments in mice that allowed them to distinguish between C3 from different sources.

When the amount of liver-produced C3 was reduced by 90%, an immunotherapy drug (anti-PD-1 antibody) remained just as effective as it was in mice with normal C3 levels.

The outcome changed when researchers stopped fibroblasts inside the tumor from producing C3. Under those conditions, the same treatment became less effective, even though the amount of circulating C3 fell by only a small amount (a 9% decrease).

"What determined the efficacy of the immunotherapy treatment was not the C3 in the blood, but the local C3 produced at the tumor site. When this C3 breaks down, it forms a fragment called iC3b that stops harmful myeloid cells from entering the tumor. As a result, immunotherapy is more likely to work," Miyai explained.

Overcoming Resistance to Immunotherapy

The team then investigated whether they could reproduce the effects of C3 in cancers that normally resist immunotherapy. They tested a drug designed to imitate the way C3 blocks myeloid cells from entering tumors.

This approach allowed immunotherapy to work against tumors that had previously resisted treatment. It also significantly extended survival in mice.

The findings could eventually help doctors identify which patients are most likely to benefit from immunotherapy. They may also lead to new treatment options for cancers that do not respond at first.

Lung Cancer Samples Support the Findings

Researchers also examined tumor samples from patients with lung cancer. Those with higher levels of C3 in the tissue surrounding cancer cells experienced better treatment results and longer survival.

About half of the patients with high local C3 levels responded to treatment. None of the patients with lower levels responded. As in the mouse studies, C3 levels in the bloodstream were not linked to treatment success.

Next Steps for Cancer Treatment Research

The researchers now plan to test ways of increasing C3 levels inside tumors and to determine the most effective timing for treatment.

They also believe that learning more about the local activity of C3 could improve understanding of other biological processes, including wound healing and the regulation of inflammation.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough in cancer immunotherapy by discovering the role of locally produced C3 protein in improving treatment efficacy and overcoming resistance. The findings have broad implications for cancer patients, potentially leading to better therapies and improved survival rates. The study is well-detailed, focusing on a single impactful topic with clear real-world benefits.

articles.title: Levitating sensor for magnetic fields could detect ultrafaint brain activity
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 06 August 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02458-9The device’s simple design could rival much more complex alternatives in biophysics research — and could even be used to search for dark matter.
articles.content:
A laser beam tracks the motions of the tiny magnet suspended in a vacuum chamber as it wobbles in response to magnetic fields.Credit: Wei Ji, Peking University

Scientists have turned a levitating magnet into a device for measuring magnetic fields, known as a magnetometer — one that is sensitive enough to detect the faint signals of the brain’s electrical activity. The technique, which is simpler than existing approaches, is reported today in Science1.

Some of the most sensitive magnetometers use looped superconducting quantum interference devices (SQUIDs), which only work at temperatures close to absolute zero and therefore require complex cryogenics. Another state-of-the-art device, called a spin-exchange relaxation-free (SERF) magnetometer, needs near-perfect shielding from external magnetic interference. Both of these requirements increase the complexity of the device and extend the distance between the sample and the magnetometer.

The levitating magnetometer described in the latest work reduces this distance to a few hundred micrometres. It is also orders of magnitude more sensitive than another type of magnetometer made from diamond.

The device is, at its heart, an exquisitely sensitive compass needle that is less than one millimetre in size. Wei Ji, a physicist at Peking University in Beijing, and his collaborators suspended the sensor magnet between a ‘lifting’ magnet above it and a diamagnet — a type of material that generates its own opposing magnetic field in response to the field of the lifting magnet — underneath it. The diamagnet therefore pushes the sensor magnet up, stabilizing it.

A laser reflects light off the sensor magnet onto a detector, measuring changes in the sensor’s orientation when a sample is brought close to the device. The whole contraption sits inside a vacuum chamber that is about the size of a Tupperware box.

Ji says that the instrument’s accuracy was achieved using an intricate combination of noise reduction techniques. Magnetic coils and damping systems reduce noise from loose magnetic fields and mechanical vibrations. “When you’re probing the femtotesla scale, even a thin film of aluminium foil can introduce 100 femtoteslas of noise,” says Ji. (A femtotesla is ten billion times weaker than Earth’s magnetic field.)
articles.reasoning: The article describes a significant technological breakthrough in magnetometer design that enables detection of ultrafaint brain activity signals with a simpler, more sensitive, and compact device. This advancement has broad implications for neuroscience research and medical diagnostics, potentially improving brain activity monitoring and understanding of neurological conditions. The device's improved sensitivity and reduced complexity represent a meaningful step forward with tangible benefits for health science.

Its design avoids the need for very cold temperatures or heavy shielding, making it easier and cheaper to use. **One-sentence takeaway** – A tiny floating magnet device offers a simpler and more sensitive way to measure faint brain activity, opening new possibilities for brain research and medical diagnosis.

articles.title: How weight-loss medication is changing relationships with alcohol
articles.summary: Some people using weight-loss drugs say their cravings for alcohol disappeared or they felt nauseous when they drank.
articles.content:
There is a growing body of research into the link between weight-loss drugs and alcohol consumption.

The drugs, with brands including Wegovy, Mounjaro and Ozempic, contain semaglutide or tirzepatide, which mimic a natural hormone called GLP-1. This suppresses appetite and keeps people feeling fuller for longer, helping them to lose weight.

Early research suggests that because these drugs affect the reward response in the brain, they can reduce cravings for substances including alcohol and nicotine, says Dr Christian Hendershot of the University of South Carolina.

He published a small-scale study, external in 2025 in which participants with alcohol use disorder craved alcohol less while taking Ozempic. Alcohol use disorder, sometimes referred to as alcoholism, is described by the NHS as drinking in a way that is harmful.

A study, external from the University of Colorado Anschutz published last week also suggested that GLP-1 medications in pill form led to fewer days of heavy drinking in people with mild to moderate alcohol use disorder.

People taking the drugs told BBC News that alcohol had affected them in different ways: some said their cravings for it had gone, drinking had made them feel nauseous or uncomfortably full, or they had got drunk more quickly. Others said they had not noticed any effect on their relationship with alcohol.

Before she started taking Wegovy, Lisa says she drank between six and eight bottles of wine a week with friends. But she had sometimes worried about whether this was too much and whether it could damage her health.

NHS guidance, external is that people should not drink more than 14 units a week on a regular basis, which is about six medium glasses of wine or six pints. Drinking too much in the long term can lead to liver damage, high blood pressure and increased risk of cancer.

Lisa says that since starting on the medication she has more than halved her consumption. At a recent day festival, she drank three glasses of wine over the course of nine hours. Previously, she would have had two bottles plus a couple of vodka mixers, she says.

Alcohol has always been a big part of her social life and when she stopped drinking for a few weeks in the late 2010s, she realised friends had stopped inviting her to social events. It led her to start drinking again.

This time round, Lisa says that she still looks forward to drinking wine, but after having a couple of glasses she simply cannot stomach any more.

"I still feel involved in things because I'm still drinking but drinking a lot less," Lisa says.

For years, Warren Thomas, 45, from Colchester, had enjoyed an occasional beer with his family after work, as well as one or two heavy drinking sessions with his friends each month.

But when he spoke to his friends on weight-loss medication about his plans to start taking Mounjaro, they warned him that it could affect how much he drank.

Warren says he noticed the effect within 24 hours of his first dose in mid-June. "I just don't want to drink," he says. "I've just got no appetite for it."

When he went out for his friend's birthday last month, he felt "light-headed and a little bit giddy" after two beers, he says.

"My tolerance level to drinking is now zero," he says.

There is no formal advice in the British National Formulary, a guide to dispensing medicine used by doctors and pharmacists, about whether people on weight-loss drugs should stop drinking alcohol, says Prof Russell Hearn, a GP and professor of medicine at King's College London.

But he gives careful advice to his patients. "Alcohol has a lot of calories in it and if your goal is to lose weight, drinking less will definitely help you with that alongside changing your diet while you're on a GLP-1," he says.

For people like Lisa and Warren, drinking less alcohol has been a happy bonus. But recent graduate Faye Goodwin, 20, feels that it has hampered her social life.

When Faye drinks she says she gets nauseous very quickly and sometimes throws up or gets bad acid reflux.

Faye, who got in touch with BBC Your Voice, has been taking Mounjaro since she was 18 and does not really know what it is like to drink alcohol without the impact of weight-loss medication. But she says she once took a month off the jabs and was able to drink without experiencing any nausea.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on emerging research showing that weight-loss medications containing GLP-1 receptor agonists may reduce alcohol cravings and consumption, which could benefit people with alcohol use disorder and improve public health. This represents a significant potential breakthrough with broad implications for addiction treatment and health outcomes. The article provides detailed context, including study findings and personal testimonies, supporting the positive real-world impact and substance of the story.

articles.title: Scientists reveal how much exercise you really need to protect your heart
articles.summary: Getting the recommended 150 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous exercise each week may offer only modest protection against heart attacks and strokes. A large study suggests that substantially greater benefits may require roughly 560 to 610 minutes a week—nearly 9 to 10 hours of brisk walking, running, cycling, or similar activity.
articles.content:
Adults may need far more weekly exercise than current guidelines recommend to achieve a major reduction in the risk of heart attack and stroke, according to findings from an observational study published online in the British Journal of Sports Medicine.

The researchers found that substantial cardiovascular protection was associated with 560 to 610 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity each week. That amount is roughly 3 to 4 times higher than the current public health recommendation of at least 150 minutes per week.

Moderate-to-vigorous activities include brisk walking, running, and cycling.

Fitness Level May Change Exercise Needs

The study also suggests that people with lower fitness levels may need slightly more exercise than highly fit individuals to receive similar cardiovascular benefits.

Based on the findings, the researchers argue that the current one-size-fits-all approach to exercise recommendations may need to be reconsidered. Instead, future guidance could include personalized activity targets based on a person's fitness level.

Cardiorespiratory fitness varies widely from one person to another and is considered a strong indicator of cardiovascular health. Poor cardiorespiratory fitness has been closely linked to a greater risk of heart attack, stroke, and early death.

One common way to measure cardiorespiratory fitness is through VO2 max, which refers to the highest rate at which the body can take in and use oxygen during intense exercise. The measurement reflects how efficiently the heart, lungs, and muscles work together to deliver and use oxygen.

Researchers Examined Exercise and VO2 Max

Researchers at Macao Polytechnic University in China investigated how physical activity and cardiorespiratory fitness, measured through estimated VO2 max, were associated with cardiovascular disease risk.

Their analysis included 17,088 people enrolled in a UK Biobank study between 2013 and 2015. Participants had an average age of 57. Of the group, 56% were female, and 96% were white.

Each participant wore a wrist device for seven consecutive days to record typical physical activity. They also completed a cycling test that was used to estimate VO2 max.

The researchers also considered smoking, alcohol use, self-rated health, diet, body mass index, resting heart rate, and blood pressure.

More Than 1,200 Cardiovascular Events Recorded

Over an average follow-up period of 7.8 years, the researchers recorded 1,233 cardiovascular events. These included 874 cases of atrial fibrillation, 156 myocardial infarctions, 111 cases of heart failure, and 92 strokes.

Adults who met the guideline of 150 minutes of exercise per week had a modest 8 to 9% lower cardiovascular risk. This association was similar across all fitness levels.

However, achieving what the researchers defined as substantial protection, meaning a reduction in risk of more than 30%, was associated with 560 to 610 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity per week.

Only 12% of participants reached that level of exercise.

Lower Fitness Was Linked to a Higher Exercise Target

People with the lowest fitness levels needed about 30 to 50 additional minutes of exercise per week compared with highly fit participants to obtain similar benefits.

For example, a 20% reduction in the risk of cardiovascular events was associated with 370 minutes of moderate to vigorous exercise per week among those with the lowest fitness. People with the highest fitness levels needed about 340 minutes per week to reach the same reduction in risk.

The researchers say, "This finding highlights the steeper challenge faced by deconditioned populations."

Study Cannot Prove Cause and Effect

Because the research was observational, it cannot establish that higher levels of exercise directly caused the lower cardiovascular risk.

The researchers also noted several limitations. The people included in the study may have been healthier and fitter than the general population. Cardiorespiratory fitness was estimated rather than measured directly, and the analysis did not assess sedentary time or lower-intensity exercise.

Even with those limitations, the researchers said the findings support current exercise guidelines as a reliable minimum level for cardiovascular protection.

At the same time, they suggested that more detailed recommendations could help motivated patients increase their activity and gain greater heart health benefits.

"Future guidelines may need to differentiate between the minimal moderate to vigorous exercise volume required for a basic safety margin and the substantially higher volumes necessary for optimal cardiovascular risk reduction," they conclude.

articles.personality_title: New study shows adults may need nearly 10 hours of exercise weekly for strong heart protection
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Current health guidelines recommend adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous exercise like brisk walking or cycling each week to protect their hearts. However, researchers wondered if this amount is enough to greatly reduce the risk of heart attacks and strokes.

**What happened** – A large study involving over 17,000 adults found that much more exercise—about 560 to 610 minutes weekly—is linked to a much stronger reduction in heart disease risk. Participants wore wrist devices to track their activity and completed fitness tests. The study followed them for nearly 8 years and recorded heart-related events.

**Impact** – The findings suggest that the current 150-minute guideline offers only modest heart protection, while close to 9 or 10 hours of exercise per week could lower risk by more than 30%. People with lower fitness levels may need even more exercise to get the same benefits. This challenges the idea that one exercise goal fits everyone and points to the need for personalized advice.

**What’s next step** – Researchers say future exercise recommendations might include different targets based on a person’s fitness level. This could help people who want better heart health know exactly how much activity they need. More research will also look at how to apply these findings to everyday life.

**One-sentence takeaway** – To greatly reduce the risk of heart attacks and strokes, adults may need several times more weekly exercise than current guidelines suggest, with personalized goals based on fitness level.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une nouvelle étude montre que presque 10 heures d’exercice par semaine protègent mieux le cœur
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les recommandations actuelles conseillent aux adultes de faire au moins 150 minutes d’exercice modéré à intense par semaine, comme la marche rapide ou le vélo, pour protéger leur cœur. Mais les chercheurs se sont demandé si cette durée suffisait vraiment à réduire fortement les risques de crises cardiaques et d’accidents vasculaires cérébraux.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Une grande étude menée auprès de plus de 17 000 adultes a montré qu’une activité beaucoup plus importante — environ 560 à 610 minutes par semaine — est liée à une réduction bien plus forte des risques cardiovasculaires. Les participants portaient des appareils au poignet pour mesurer leur activité et ont passé des tests de forme physique. L’étude a duré près de 8 ans et a enregistré des événements cardiaques.

**Impact** – Les résultats suggèrent que les 150 minutes recommandées offrent seulement une protection modeste, tandis que près de 9 à 10 heures d’exercice par semaine peuvent diminuer le risque de plus de 30 %. Les personnes moins en forme pourraient avoir besoin d’encore plus d’exercice pour obtenir les mêmes bénéfices. Cela remet en question l’idée d’un objectif unique pour tous et propose un conseil personnalisé.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs indiquent que les futures recommandations pourraient fixer des objectifs différents selon le niveau de forme physique. Cela aiderait ceux qui veulent améliorer leur santé cardiaque à savoir exactement combien d’activité pratiquer. D’autres recherches étudieront comment appliquer ces résultats dans la vie quotidienne.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Pour réduire fortement les risques de crises cardiaques et d’AVC, les adultes pourraient devoir faire plusieurs fois plus d’exercice chaque semaine que ce que recommandent les directives actuelles, avec des objectifs personnalisés selon leur forme physique.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevo estudio muestra que los adultos necesitan casi 10 horas de ejercicio semanal para proteger mejor el corazón
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Las pautas actuales recomiendan que los adultos hagan al menos 150 minutos de ejercicio moderado a intenso por semana, como caminar rápido o andar en bicicleta, para proteger el corazón. Sin embargo, los investigadores se preguntaron si esta cantidad es suficiente para reducir mucho el riesgo de ataques cardíacos y derrames cerebrales.

**Qué pasó** – Un gran estudio con más de 17,000 adultos encontró que mucho más ejercicio — entre 560 y 610 minutos a la semana — está relacionado con una reducción mucho mayor del riesgo cardiovascular. Los participantes usaron dispositivos en la muñeca para registrar su actividad y realizaron pruebas de condición física. El estudio los siguió durante casi 8 años y registró eventos relacionados con el corazón.

**Impacto** – Los resultados sugieren que la recomendación de 150 minutos ofrece solo una protección modesta, mientras que cerca de 9 o 10 horas de ejercicio semanal pueden reducir el riesgo en más del 30%. Las personas con menor nivel de condición física podrían necesitar aún más ejercicio para obtener los mismos beneficios. Esto cuestiona la idea de una meta única para todos y señala la necesidad de consejos personalizados.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores dicen que las futuras recomendaciones podrían incluir objetivos diferentes según el nivel de condición física de cada persona. Esto podría ayudar a quienes quieren mejorar su salud cardíaca a saber exactamente cuánto ejercicio necesitan. También se realizarán más estudios para aplicar estos hallazgos en la vida diaria.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Para reducir mucho el riesgo de ataques cardíacos y derrames, los adultos podrían necesitar varias veces más ejercicio semanal del que sugieren las pautas actuales, con metas personalizadas según su nivel de condición física.
